lessons.title: How to Compare Your Tax Under Both Regimes Step by Step

children.text: You now know every rule that matters. This lesson turns those rules into a method you can run on your own salary in fifteen minutes with a payslip, a rent agreement and a calculator. We will build it step by step, then run it end to end on one real-world salary structure.

body.text: Never compare regimes by counting deductions. Compute the final tax under both rulebooks, line by line, and compare the two numbers. Anything else is guesswork.

body.latex: \text{Old taxable} = \text{Gross salary} - \text{HRA} - \text{LTA} - 50{,}000 - \text{PT} - \text{Home loan interest} + \text{Other income} - \text{80C, 80CCD, 80D, 80TTA, etc.}
body.caption: PT is professional tax. Home loan interest is for a self-occupied house, capped at ₹2,00,000.
Much shorter, which is exactly the point of the new regime.

children.text: List every income for the tax year: gross salary including employer NPS, FD and savings interest, dividends and rent. Keep capital gains on shares aside, since they are taxed at special rates (covered in Lesson 4 of this chapter).
Old regime, salary: subtract HRA and LTA exemptions, the ₹50,000 standard deduction and professional tax.
Old regime, other heads: add interest and other income, and subtract home loan interest on a self-occupied house. The result is gross total income.
Old regime, deductions: subtract 80C, 80CCD(1B), 80CCD(2), 80D, 80TTA and any others from gross total income. The result is old regime taxable income.
New regime: take gross salary, subtract ₹75,000, add other income, and subtract employer NPS. The result is new regime taxable income.
For each regime, apply its slabs, then the rebate or marginal relief, then 4% cess.
Compare the two totals, then sanity-check: is every deduction you used genuine and backed by a document?

body.title: Where Do Deductions Come Off?
body.textWithBlank: Deductions like 80C and 80D are subtracted from ___ total income to arrive at taxable income.
body.explanation: First you compute income under each head, such as salary after exemptions and interest income, and add them up to get gross total income. Deductions like 80C and 80D come off that figure.

children.text: Neelam, 32, is a product designer at a Bengaluru fintech. Her annual salary is: basic ₹9,00,000, HRA ₹3,60,000, LTA ₹50,000, special allowance ₹5,40,000 and employer NPS of ₹90,000 (10% of basic). She pays ₹30,000 a month rent in Koramangala, flew home to Lucknow this year for ₹32,000, and her employer deducts ₹2,500 of professional tax. Her EPF contribution is ₹1,08,000, she invests ₹42,000 in ELSS and pays ₹18,000 for health insurance. She also earned ₹40,000 of FD interest and ₹8,000 of savings account interest.

body.title: Show me the math behind each line

children.text: HRA: least of HRA received (₹3,60,000), rent minus 10% of basic (₹3,60,000 minus ₹90,000, which is ₹2,70,000), and 40% of basic for Bengaluru (₹3,60,000). Exemption: ₹2,70,000.
LTA: ₹50,000 received, but only the ₹32,000 fare is exempt. The balance ₹18,000 stays in taxable salary.

body.text: Neelam claims ₹6.2 lakh of genuine old regime benefits, including a sizeable Bengaluru rent, and the new regime still wins by over ₹60,000. The new regime's lower slabs on ₹18 lakh of income are simply worth more than her deductions. The next lesson shows you how to find the exact deduction level where this flips.

body.title: Bonus: what if Neelam restructures to 14% employer NPS?

children.text: In the new regime she can raise employer NPS from 10% to 14% of basic, which is ₹1,26,000. Restructuring is CTC-neutral, so her special allowance falls by ₹36,000 and gross salary stays at ₹19,40,000. New regime taxable income drops by ₹36,000 to ₹17,87,000.
Slab tax becomes ₹1,20,000 plus 20% of ₹1,87,000 (₹37,400), total ₹1,57,400. Cess ₹6,296. Total ₹1,63,696, a further saving of ₹7,488 a year, taking the gap over the old regime to ₹67,964.

body.title: Run the New Regime Side
body.prompt: Tarun, a civil engineer at an infrastructure firm in Nagpur, has a gross salary of ₹16,00,000 and ₹25,000 of FD interest. His employer does not contribute to NPS. What is his total new regime tax including cess?
body.explanation: Taxable income is ₹16,00,000 minus ₹75,000 plus ₹25,000, which is ₹15,50,000. Slab tax is ₹60,000 up to ₹12 lakh plus 15% of ₹3,50,000 (₹52,500), total ₹1,12,500. No rebate or marginal relief applies. Cess is ₹4,500. Total: ₹1,17,000.

children.text: The Five Mistakes That Wreck a Comparison

cells: Using ₹50,000 standard deduction in both regimes
Forgetting employer NPS on the new side
EPF already sits inside the ₹1.5 lakh 80C cap
Add EPF to other 80C items, then cap at ₹1,50,000
FD interest is taxable in both regimes and can push you over ₹12 lakh
Pull interest figures from your AIS
Only the least of three limits is exempt

body.title: Spot the Error
body.question: Harsh's comparison shows new regime taxable income of ₹12,20,000, calculated as gross salary ₹13,45,000 minus ₹75,000 minus ₹50,000 of 80CCD(1B) NPS. He has no other income or employer NPS. What is his correct new regime taxable income?
options: ₹12,70,000, because 80CCD(1B) is not allowed in the new regime
body.explanation: Only employer NPS under 80CCD(2) survives in the new regime. His own ₹50,000 NPS contribution under 80CCD(1B) does not. Correct taxable income is ₹13,45,000 minus ₹75,000, which is ₹12,70,000.

body.title: Meghna Trusts the HR Portal
body.scenario: Meghna works at a Kolkata IT services firm. Her HR portal shows a neat side-by-side: old regime tax ₹1,05,000, new regime tax ₹98,000, recommendation 'New Regime'. She also earns ₹2,20,000 of rent from a flat in Salt Lake on which she pays ₹3,10,000 of home loan interest, and ₹90,000 of FD interest.
body.prompt: Should she accept the portal's recommendation as final?
body.modelAnswer: No. The employer's calculator only knows her salary and the declarations she submits. It does not know about her FD interest or her let-out flat unless she declares them. The FD interest raises tax in both regimes. The let-out flat is the bigger issue: after the 30% standard deduction on rent and the interest, it creates a house property loss. In the old regime up to ₹2 lakh of that loss is set off against her salary, while in the new regime the loss lapses. That could reverse the recommendation. She should rerun the full seven-step comparison including all income, then declare the regime that actually wins.

body.text: This method covers most salaried taxpayers. Two situations need extra steps: capital gains on shares or mutual funds, which are taxed at special rates and do not get the rebate, and income above ₹50 lakh, where surcharge applies at different maximum rates in each regime. Both are covered in Lesson 4 of this chapter.

body.title: Run Your Own Comparison
steps: Download your AIS from the income tax e-filing portal to capture all interest and dividend income
Write down each salary component from your payslip, including employer NPS
Calculate HRA using the least-of-three formula and LTA using actual fares
Total your 80C items and cap them at ₹1,50,000
Complete the old regime column line by line
Complete the new regime column with ₹75,000 standard deduction and employer NPS only
Apply slabs, rebate or marginal relief, and 4% cess to both, then compare

body.label: Income Tax Department Tax Calculator
body.description: Once you have done the comparison by hand, cross-check your numbers against the official calculator on the e-filing portal.

points: Compare regimes by computing final tax under both, never by counting deductions.
Old regime taxable income runs through exemptions, standard deduction, professional tax, house property, then Chapter deductions.
New regime taxable income is gross salary minus ₹75,000, plus other income, minus employer NPS.
Apply slabs, then the rebate or marginal relief, then 4% cess, separately for each regime.
Include all income, especially FD interest and rental income, which your employer's calculator may not see.
Capital gains and incomes above ₹50 lakh need extra steps covered later in this chapter.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not tax advice. Figures reflect the rules applicable to tax year 2026-27 as understood at the time of writing, for resident individuals without surcharge. Examples are illustrative. Consult a qualified tax professional before filing.
